subject: A question about clone correction on SNP data

messages.author: 752aaa009ee55b1c
messages.subject: A question about clone correction on SNP data
parts:
Dear Zhian,

Here I am with another question for you. I am trying to perform clone correction on my SNP data.

A few months ago, someone analyzed a subpopulation of my samples using microsatellite data (12 loci); when performing clone correction with POPPR reduced the genotypes from 21 to 9;

I have now whole genome SNPs (13,000 SNPs) for the same isolates; when performing a phylogenetic analysis the topology of the clade for that subpopulation matches the 9 main lineages identified with microsatellites clone correction (i.e. some samples are almost identical).

When using clonecorrect() on these data the number of (diploid) genotypes is identical to the number of individuals. I wonder if you think it's worth to use filter_stats, or I should just be happy with the fact that increasing the level of detail (i.e. from 12 ms markers to 13K SNPs), the individuals are just different.
What I did:
testfilter<-filter_stats(
  x = wwDiploid13k_missing005,
  distance = bitwise.dist, plot = TRUE)



This is the result:

I can see a very steep peak around 0.001 (verified with abline()), but I am not sure I am interpreting it correctly.
Maybe I am just overthinking it, I am new to POPPR and trying to find my way around.

Thank you for your kind attention,
Max

messages.author: d192ec4b1d416345
messages.subject: Re: [poppr] A question about clone correction on SNP data
parts:
Hello,

In regards to your question:

When using clonecorrect() on these data the number of (diploid) genotypes is identical to the number of individuals. I wonder if you think it's worth to use filter_stats, or I should just be happy with the fact that increasing the level of detail (i.e. from 12 ms markers to 13K SNPs), the individuals are just different.

Short answer: Yes, use mlg.filter() to collapse genotypes into lineages (Disclaimer: this is unless you have absolutely perfect sequences and consider each new mutation as a separate lineage). 

I've written a small example of how to choose a cutoff threshold here: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/poppr/vignettes/mlg.html#choosing-a-threshold. For comparisons between the performance of microsatellite markers and SNP markers to detect clonal lineages, see Rafiei et al. 2017: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/ppa.12713 

Additionally, if things are moving a bit slow or taking up a lot of memory on your machine, you may want to consider using the snpclone/genlight object to store your data in your R session; it's 8 times more memory efficient with the caveat that it assumes biallelic SNPs. If your data are in PLINK or VCF format, then there is the adegenet::read.PLINK() and vcfR::read.vcfR()/vcfR::vcfR2genlight() functions. 

Hope that helps!
Zhian

messages.subject: Re: [poppr] A question about clone correction on SNP data
parts:
Hi, Zhian,

Thank you for the extensive answer, I am going through the literature and trying to run RClone.
I also went through the tutorial regarding choosing thresholds with cutoff_predictor().
Since the plot generated by filter_stats was covered by the legend, I re-drew it myself:

plot(x = statsfilter$farthest$THRESHOLDS, y = 169:1, col='red',
     xlab= 'Genetic Distance Cutoff',
     ylab='Number of Multilocus Lineages')
points(x = statsfilter$average$THRESHOLDS, y = 169:1, col='blue')
points(x = statsfilter$nearest$THRESHOLDS, y = 169:1, col='green')
legend(0.09, 150, legend=c("Farthest", "UPGMA", "Nearest"),
       fill = c("red", "blue", "green"), cex=0.75)



Hope it makes sense, the plot looks the same.

Choosing the threshold by eye, I would say there is a steep increase for genetic distances < 0.001 (red vertical line), for a total of 151 unique genotypes. When using cutoff_predictor, the threshold is 0.0122 (blue line), which visually does not seem very intuitive, although the result is almost identical (149 unique genotypes).

Then I use mlg.id to identify the clone groups. Would you say that my analysis makes sense? I wouldn't want to ask you for the interpretation of my results, but I am trying to understand if I am using the tool properly and what I see makes sense.

EDIT: Thinking back, it does make sense to keep 149 samples (as per cutoff_predictor), it is evident that going below 0.0122 there is a long gap before start losing genotypes again. So I will keep the threshold such as to keep 149 contracted multilocus genotypes.

Thank you again for POPPR and for your kind attention,
Max

messages.author: d192ec4b1d416345
messages.subject: Re: [poppr] A question about clone correction on SNP data
parts: Hi Max,
Would you say that my analysis makes sense?
I'd say that what you've presented so far makes sense.

Choosing the threshold by eye, I would say there is a steep increase for genetic distances < 0.001 (red vertical line), for a total of 151 unique genotypes. When using cutoff_predictor, the threshold is 0.0122 (blue line), which visually does not seem very intuitive, although the result is almost identical (149 unique genotypes).

cutoff_predictor() is kind of ham-fisted. All it wants to do is to find the largest gap between points on the left side of the plot and draw a line down the middle of it. That being said, it does work pretty well. The rationale behind it is that you set the threshold high enough to retain all the possible mutations encountered in a multilocus lineage but low enough that you don't drag in sister clades. Additionally, the problem with choosing a threshold by eye from the histogram is that histograms are also ham-fisted ways of representing data, so the analysis by eye may be different with a different representation of the data ¯\_(ツ)_/¯.

Of course, this all gets into the question of "What is a clone, anyways?", and your choice of threshold ultimately depends on that definition and how much stock you put into your markers.

But, I digress; your analysis thusfar seems perfectly fine to me!

Cheers,
Zhian
